title: Convolutional Neural Networks
subtitle: Contact session 6 · T1 Chapters 7–8 · convolution, padding, stride, pooling, parameters, classic architectures and transfer learning

lesson.title: Why not a plain MLP for images?
lesson.lead: Images are huge, and objects can appear **anywhere**. CNNs exploit locality and reuse the same filter everywhere.

items: A 50 × 50 image is already 2,500 inputs; a 1920 × 1080 HD image is about 2 million per channel.
**Invariance:** a cat is a cat wherever it sits in the frame.
**Locality:** small patterns (edges, eyes) don't need the whole image.
**Sub-sampling:** shrinking an image doesn't change the object.

blocks.text: Three key principles

head: Principle
Meaning
rows: Each neuron sees only a small region: its receptive field
The same filter slides over the whole input, so far fewer parameters
Shift the input and the feature map shifts the same way

blocks.text: Tasks: image classification, face detection, object recognition, image captioning, segmentation.

lesson.title: The CNN pipeline
lesson.lead: **INPUT → [CONV → ReLU → POOL] × N → FLATTEN → FC → SOFTMAX**

blocks.text: Example (LeNet-style): 32×32×3 → conv 5×5, 6 filters → 28×28×6 → pool → 14×14×6 → conv 5×5, 16 filters → 10×10×16 → pool → 5×5×16 → FC → output.

head: Layers
Learn
rows: Combine all features into class scores

blocks.label: Design pattern
blocks.text: Pattern to remember: as you go deeper, **spatial size shrinks and channel depth grows** (224×224×3 → … → 14×14×512).

lesson.title: The convolution operation
lesson.lead: Slide the filter, multiply element-wise, add up (plus bias): one number per position.

blocks.text: (I ⋆ K)(i, j) = Σₘ Σₙ I(i + m, j + n) · K(m, n) + b
blocks.caption: deep learning frameworks actually compute cross-correlation but call it convolution

items: Start at the top-left corner.
Multiply element-wise and sum.
Slide right by the stride s.
At the end of a row, jump down by s to the leftmost position.
The filter must fit **completely** inside the input, never partly.

blocks.text: The 6 × 6 image below with the diagonal filter (1 on the diagonal, −1 elsewhere) gives a 4 × 4 feature map whose top-left value is **3**: the diagonal pattern is strongly present.
The kernel values are **learned** by backpropagation. Trained first-layer kernels look like edge detectors, e.g. vertical [[−1, 0, 1], [−1, 0, 1], [−1, 0, 1]].

blocks.caption: n = input size, k = kernel, p = padding, s = stride

head: Padding
Effect
rows: p = (k − 1)/2 with s = 1, so output = input

blocks.text: Stride vs dilation
A 3 × 3 kernel with r = 2 covers 5 × 5 with only 9 weights.

lesson.title: Channels and parameters
lesson.lead: A filter is as **deep as its input**; the number of filters is the number of output channels.

blocks.text: parameters = (K × K × Cᵢₙ + 1) × Cₒᵤₜ
blocks.caption: independent of the image's height and width

items: Multi-channel: convolve each channel with its own kernel slice, then **sum across channels** plus one bias → one feature map.
5 × 5 filters, 3 input channels, 64 filters: (75 + 1) × 64 = **4,864**.
Pooling layers have **0** parameters (only hyperparameters k and s).

blocks.text: Receptive field
RF_l = RF_{l−1} + (K_l − 1) × Πᵢ<l Sᵢ
blocks.caption: stacked 3×3, stride 1: 3 → 5 → 7 → 9

blocks.label: Why small kernels
blocks.text: Two stacked 3 × 3 convs see 5 × 5 with 18 weights per channel pair instead of 25, and add an extra non-linearity. That's why VGG uses only 3 × 3.

lesson.title: Pooling, ReLU and 1×1 convolutions
lesson.lead: Pooling downsamples with **no parameters**; a 1×1 conv mixes channels cheaply.

head: Pooling
Output
Note
rows: Most common; keeps the strongest activation

blocks.text: Pooling gives translation invariance, reduces computation and acts as mild regularisation. Max-pool 2 × 2, s = 2: 4 × 4 → 2 × 2.
ReLU is applied after each conv: cheap, non-saturating for positive inputs, gives sparse activations, scale-invariant. Downsides: dying ReLU, not zero-centred.
1×1 convolution ("network in network")

items: A weighted sum **across channels** at each pixel: no spatial context.
Reduces channels (256 → 64), adds non-linearity, cuts computation.

blocks.caption: about 12× fewer weights: the bottleneck design

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide prints 147,456 for the bottleneck and calls it 11×. The arithmetic gives 135,168 (≈ 12×). If this comes up, show your sum.

lesson.title: Fully connected head and softmax
lesson.lead: Flatten the final maps, then a dense layer y = f(Wx + b) maps features to class scores.

blocks.text: FC layers are parameter-heavy, lose spatial structure and need a fixed input size. Modern alternatives: global average pooling and 1×1 convs.

lesson.title: Classic architectures
lesson.lead: Each landmark network added one idea that is still used today.

head: Network
Year
Key ideas
Size
rows: First successful CNN; conv-pool-conv-pool-FC; tanh/sigmoid; average pooling; MNIST
ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, GPUs, LRN; 5 conv + 3 FC; won ImageNet (top-5 error 15.3%)
Only 3×3 conv (s 1, p 1) and 2×2 max-pool; 13 conv + 3 FC; simple and deep
MLPconv (1×1 convs), global average pooling replaces FC
Parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5, pool branches, concatenated; 1×1 bottlenecks; 22 layers; auxiliary classifiers
Residual blocks y = F(x) + x; skip connections; 50–152 layers; won ImageNet 2015 (3.6%)

blocks.text: Inception's 1×1 reduction cut one module from about 390M to 118M operations (3.3×). Factorisation (v3): 5×5 → two 3×3 (28% fewer operations); 3×3 → 3×1 + 1×3.

lesson.title: ResNet and residual learning
lesson.lead: Learn the **residual** F(x) = H(x) − x, so the block outputs **y = F(x) + x**.

blocks.text: The surprise: a 56-layer plain network had **higher training error** than an 18-layer one. Not overfitting, but an optimisation problem (degradation).

items: If the identity is the best mapping, the block only has to push F(x) to 0, which is easy.
**Gradient highway:** ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · (1 + ∂F/∂x); the "1" always lets the gradient through.
It behaves like an ensemble of 2ⁿ paths; earlier features are reused.
Dimension mismatch is handled by a **projection shortcut**: a 1×1 conv with stride 2.

lesson.title: Design, transfer learning and tips
lesson.lead: Start from a proven network and **transfer** it whenever you can.

head: Strategy
What you train
When
rows: Only the new classifier; conv layers frozen

items: Always: spatial reduction + channel expansion. Deep networks: skip connections. Tight budget: bottlenecks (MobileNet, EfficientNet).
Underfitting → add depth or width. Overfitting → data augmentation, dropout, L2 before shrinking the model.
Depth vs width: deeper gives more complex features but is harder to train; wider is easier and faster. EfficientNet scales depth, width and resolution together.
Practical: normalise pixels, augment (flip, crop, rotate, colour jitter), batch norm, early stopping, gradient clipping.

blocks.text: Beyond classification: detection (R-CNN family, YOLO, SSD), segmentation (FCN, U-Net, DeepLab), face recognition, style transfer, super-resolution, 1-D convs for audio and time series.
